section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: Those who knew Jesus called him a man and a prophet

rows.thesis: The people closest to Jesus, including his own disciples after the resurrection, described him as a man and a prophet sent by God, not as God.
rows.arg:
P1 If Jesus had taught that he was God, his disciples and the earliest preachers would describe him that way. 
 P2 Instead, the Gospels and Acts repeatedly describe him as "a prophet" and "a man approved by God", including in the first public sermon of the church. 
 ∴ The earliest witnesses did not understand Jesus to be God.
rows.ev:
The crowds: "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee" (Matt 21:11); "a great prophet has arisen among us; God has visited His people" (Luke 7:16).

 The disciples on the road to Emmaus, after the crucifixion, describe him as "a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people" (Luke 24:19).

 Jesus about himself: "you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God" (John 8:40).

 Peter's first sermon at Pentecost, the founding proclamation of the church: "Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him" (Acts 2:22). Notice who does the miracles: God, through him.

 Others in John call him a prophet: the Samaritan woman (4:19), the crowd after the feeding (6:14, "truly the Prophet who is to come into the world"), the crowd at the feast (7:40), the blind man (9:17).

 
 Mainstream scholarship agrees that the Synoptic Gospels do not present Jesus as God. James Dunn, a believing Christian scholar, concludes that there is no clear indication in the earliest traditions that Jesus thought of himself as divine, and that the Christian worship of Jesus did not take the form of cultic worship ( latreia ) given to God.

 Tap to enlarge James Dunn, Did the First Christians Worship Jesus? : cultic worship (latreia) is never offered to Christ in the New Testament

مَّا الْمَسِيحُ ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ مِن قَبْلِهِ الرُّسُلُ وَأُمُّهُ صِدِّيقَةٌ ۖ كَانَا يَأْكُلَانِ الطَّعَامَ
 5:75
rows.obj:
"Calling him a prophet doesn't exclude him being God; he's both."
 Then the earliest sermon was the moment to say so. Peter is explaining who Jesus is to thousands of Jews, and the description he gives is "a man" through whom God worked. The two-natures doctrine is a later formulation (Chalcedon, 451) read back into texts that never state it.


 "These are the views of people who didn't yet understand."
 Acts 2 is after the resurrection and after the Spirit was given, at the moment the apostles are said to be filled with understanding. If they still described him as a man attested by God, that is the apostolic understanding.

 Answer it in your head first, then compare.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: Jesus distinguishes himself from the one true God

rows.thesis: In his own words, Jesus places himself under God, calls the Father "the only true God", and calls God "my God".
rows.arg:
P1 If Jesus were God, he would not deny goodness to himself, call someone else "the only true God", or say that he has a God. 
 P2 Jesus does all three (Mark 10:18; John 17:3; John 20:17), and says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). 
 ∴ Jesus did not present himself as God.
rows.ev:
"Why do you call me good?" When a man addressed him as "Good Teacher", Jesus answered: "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19). This was so uncomfortable that Matthew, copying Mark, rewrote it: "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good" (Matt 19:17). Early Christian writers knew a form of the saying that is even clearer: "One is good, my Father in heaven" (Justin, Dialogue 101; Irenaeus; Hippolytus; Origen, Contra Celsum 5.11; the Clementine Homilies), as W.L. Petersen documents. The point is not that Jesus was morally bad; Barnabas is called "a good man" (Acts 11:24). It is that Jesus reserves God's absolute goodness for God alone and refuses to share it.

 Tap to enlarge W.L. Petersen: early fathers quote the saying as "One is good, my Father in heaven" (Mark 10:18 / Matt 19:17) 
 "The only true God". In his prayer Jesus says: "This is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent" (John 17:3). The Father is "the only true God"; Jesus is the one sent. This sentence is so clear that Augustine had to rearrange it to read "that they may know You and Jesus Christ whom You have sent as the only true God" ( Tractates on John 105). The same structure appears in 1 Corinthians 8:6: "for us there is one God, the Father… and one Lord, Jesus Christ".

 "My God and your God". After the resurrection Jesus says to Mary Magdalene: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17). In Revelation, the risen Jesus says "my God" four times in one verse (Rev 3:12). God has no God.

 Dependence. "The Son can do nothing of himself, but only what he sees the Father doing" (John 5:19); "I can do nothing on my own… I seek not my own will but the will of Him who sent me" (5:30); "the Father is greater than I" (14:28); "my teaching is not mine but His who sent me" (7:16).
rows.ar:
مَا قُلْتُ لَهُمْ إِلَّا مَا أَمَرْتَنِي بِهِ أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبَّكُمْ
 5:117 
 وَإِنَّ اللَّهَ رَبِّي وَرَبُّكُمْ فَاعْبُدُوهُ ۚ هَٰذَا صِرَاطٌ مُّسْتَقِيمٌ
 19:36
rows.obj:
"In Mark 10:18 Jesus is testing the man: 'If you call me good, realise I'm God.'"
 Nothing in the passage says so, and Matthew clearly did not read it that way, because he changed it. The early fathers quoted it to show the Father's unique goodness. An interpretation that needs a hidden meaning the earliest readers missed is weak.


 "'The Father is greater' refers to Jesus' human nature only."
 That is a later distinction (the two-natures doctrine). In the text Jesus says " I ", the whole person. And the same "human nature only" move can explain away any verse, which makes the doctrine unfalsifiable. If every verse that limits Jesus is "his human nature", the evidence never gets to count.


 "John 17:3 just means the Father is true God; Jesus is too."
 Then the word "only" means nothing. "You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You sent" lists two parties with two different descriptions.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Jesus said "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30).”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The word "one" is neuter ( hen ), meaning one in purpose, not one person or being. Jesus prays that his disciples "may be one ( hen ) just as we are one" (John 17:22). And when the Jews accused him of making himself God after 10:30, he answered by quoting Psalm 82:6, where human judges are called "gods", and said he had only called himself "Son of God" (10:34-36).
rows.sum: Jesus refuses to be called good in God's sense, calls the Father "the only true God", calls the Father "my God" after the resurrection, and says he can do nothing by himself. His own words place him under God.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: Jesus lacked the attributes of God

rows.thesis: God is all-knowing, cannot be tempted, does not grow, and cannot die. The Gospels show Jesus did not know the Hour, grew in wisdom, was tempted, and died.
rows.arg:
P1 Whoever lacks an essential attribute of God is not God. 
 P2 Jesus lacked omniscience (Mark 13:32), immutability (Luke 2:52), the impossibility of being tempted (James 1:13 vs Hebrews 4:15), and immortality (1 Timothy 6:16 vs his death). 
 ∴ Jesus is not God.
rows.ev:
Ignorance of the Hour. "Concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father" (Mark 13:32). The verse troubled the church so much that scribes deleted "nor the Son" from the parallel in Matthew 24:36 in many manuscripts, as Metzger and Ehrman document, and Luke leaves the saying out. Ambrose claimed the phrase was an Arian interpolation; Jerome noted it was missing in some Greek copies. Later the church condemned the "Agnoetae", who taught that Christ was ignorant of some things, even though earlier fathers such as Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus and Cyril had attributed ignorance to his humanity.

 Tap to enlarge Metzger & Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament : scribes dropped "nor the Son" from Matthew 24:36 to protect Jesus' divinity 
 Some apologists say oiden ("knows") here means "declares". No Greek lexicon gives that meaning; the context is a parable about watchfulness because no one knows ; and if "know" meant "declare", the angels would be forbidden to declare it, yet in Revelation 14:6-7 an angel announces "the hour of His judgement has come". Other passages show the same limit: he went to a fig tree "to see if he could find anything on it" and found nothing because "it was not the season for figs" (Mark 11:13).

 Growth. "Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature" (Luke 2:52). God does not increase in wisdom.

 Temptation. "God cannot be tempted with evil" (James 1:13); Jesus "was tempted in every way as we are" (Hebrews 4:15), and was tempted by Satan for forty days (Matt 4).

 Death. God "alone has immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16) and is "the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God" (1 Tim 1:17). Jesus died, and "Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father" (Rom 6:4); God raised him (Acts 2:24, 32). The one who dies is not the immortal one, and the one who is raised is not the one who raises.

 Prayer and need. Jesus prayed all night (Luke 6:12), asked for the cup to pass from him and submitted: "not my will but Yours" (Luke 22:42), and was strengthened by an angel (22:43).
rows.ar:
تَعْلَمُ مَا فِي نَفْسِي وَلَا أَعْلَمُ مَا فِي نَفْسِكَ ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ
 5:116
rows.obj:
"He limited himself voluntarily (kenosis) while on earth."
 If he set aside omniscience, then during his ministry he was not omniscient, and a being who is not omniscient is not God at that time. God cannot stop being God. And Revelation 1:1 says the revelation was given to the risen Jesus by God, so even after the resurrection he receives knowledge.


 "These limits belong to his human nature; his divine nature knew."
 Then one person both knew and did not know the Hour at the same moment, which is a contradiction in a single mind. And when Jesus said "not even the Son", he did not say "not even my human nature".
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “God can do anything, so He can become a man who doesn't know things.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Omnipotence means power over every possible thing, not over contradictions. "An all-knowing being who doesn't know the Hour" is a contradiction, like a square circle. God can create a man and give him knowledge; He cannot be ignorant and remain God.
rows.sum: Jesus did not know the Hour, grew in wisdom, was tempted, prayed for help and died. God knows all, never changes, cannot be tempted and alone is immortal. The scribes who altered Matthew 24:36 knew how serious the problem was.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: The main proof texts are textually insecure

rows.thesis: Several of the clearest "Jesus is God" verses are later scribal changes or depend on disputed punctuation, which shows that later Christians felt the original text was not clear enough.
rows.arg:
P1 A doctrine as central as Jesus' deity should rest on texts whose wording is secure. 
 P2 Several of the strongest proof texts (1 John 5:7, 1 Timothy 3:16, Acts 20:28, Romans 9:5) are either later additions, variants, or matters of punctuation added by editors, and the direction of change is always toward higher Christology. 
 ∴ The proof texts cannot bear the weight placed on them, and scribal changes show the doctrine shaped the text, not the other way round.
rows.ev:
1 John 5:7 (the "Johannine Comma"). "There are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one" (KJV). It is absent from all Greek manuscripts before the late Middle Ages and from all the early versions. Modern translations remove it. It is the only explicit Trinity verse in the Bible, and it is a forgery.

 1 Timothy 3:16. The KJV reads " God was manifest in the flesh". The earliest manuscripts read " who was manifested". In Greek capitals the difference is a stroke: ΟΣ ("who") became ΘΣ, the abbreviation for "God". Metzger's Textual Commentary (p. 641) says the change arose either by accident or deliberately to give "greater dogmatic precision".

 Acts 20:28. "The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood". Several important manuscripts read "the church of the Lord ". Even with "God", the Greek dia tou haimatos tou idiou most naturally means "with the blood of His own [one]", that is His own Son, just as Romans 8:32 says God "did not spare His own Son".

 Romans 9:5. "Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever" depends entirely on punctuation, which the original manuscripts did not have. The RSV and others punctuate it as a separate praise of the Father: "…the Christ. God who is over all be blessed for ever." Paul never elsewhere calls Jesus "God over all"; for him "God" is the Father (1 Cor 8:6).

 John 1:18. Manuscripts divide between "the only-begotten Son " and "the only-begotten God ". Both readings are early; neither is secure enough to build a doctrine on.

 
 Tap to enlarge Metzger: a corrector in Codex Vaticanus wrote "Fool and knave, leave the old reading, don't change it!", showing how freely scribes altered the text
rows.obj:
"The Trinity doesn't depend on the Comma; scholars agree it's spurious."
 Good, then the question becomes why it was added, and why the KJV tradition defended it for centuries. It shows that the church felt the need for an explicit text that the authentic NT does not provide.


 "There are still enough verses."
 Then the case should be made from texts like John 17:3 and Mark 10:18, which are secure and say the opposite. The fact that the direction of corruption always runs toward a "higher" Jesus is evidence about how the doctrine developed.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Textual variants don't change any doctrine. Every major doctrine is supported by secure texts.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The examples show the opposite pressure: scribes changed "who" to "God", added "these three are one", and deleted "nor the Son". Even Ehrman's The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture documents changes made for theological reasons. A text being altered to support a doctrine suggests the doctrine was not secure in the original.
rows.sum: The Johannine Comma is a late forgery, "God" in 1 Timothy 3:16 was originally "who", Acts 20:28 has variants and means "the blood of His own", and Romans 9:5 depends on modern punctuation. Each change moved toward a higher Christology.

Metzger's Textual Commentary (p. 641) says the change arose either by accident or deliberately to give "greater dogmatic precision".

 Acts 20:28. "The church of God, which he obtained with his own blood". Several important manuscripts read "the church of the Lord ". Even with "God", the Greek dia tou haimatos tou idiou most naturally means "with the blood of His own [one]", that is His own Son, just as Romans 8:32 says God "did not spare His own Son".

 Romans 9:5. "Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever" depends entirely on punctuation, which the original manuscripts did not have. The RSV and others punctuate it as a separate praise of the Father: "…the Christ. God who is over all be blessed for ever." Paul never elsewhere calls Jesus "God over all"; for him "God" is the Father (1 Cor 8:6).

 John 1:18. Manuscripts divide between "the only-begotten Son " and "the only-begotten God ". Both readings are early; neither is secure enough to build a doctrine on.

 
 Tap to enlarge Metzger: a corrector in Codex Vaticanus wrote "Fool and knave, leave the old reading, don't change it!", showing how freely scribes altered the text 


 Objections
 "The Trinity doesn't depend on the Comma; scholars agree it's spurious."
 Good, then the question becomes why it was added, and why the KJV tradition defended it for centuries. It shows that the church felt the need for an explicit text that the authentic NT does not provide.


 "There are still enough verses."
 Then the case should be made from texts like John 17:3 and Mark 10:18, which are secure and say the opposite. The fact that the direction of corruption always runs toward a "higher" Jesus is evidence about how the doctrine developed.

 Your opponent says
 “Textual variants don't change any doctrine. Every major doctrine is supported by secure texts.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The examples show the opposite pressure: scribes changed "who" to "God", added "these three are one", and deleted "nor the Son". section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: John 1:1: "the Word was God" does not mean Jesus is the one God

rows.thesis: John 1:1 distinguishes "the God" (ho theos) from the Word, who is "god" (theos) without the article. Early Christians, including Origen, read it as making the Word divine but subordinate, which is heresy by later standards.
rows.arg:
P1 If John 1:1 taught that the Word is the one God, the earliest interpreters would have read it that way. 
 P2 The text says the Word was "with the God" ( pros ton theon ) and then "the Word was god " ( theos , no article). Origen and the second-century fathers read it as making the Word a derived, lesser divinity. 
 ∴ John 1:1 does not teach that the Word is the one true God; at most it teaches a subordinate divine being, which neither Islam nor Nicene Christianity accepts.
rows.ev:
The Greek. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God ( ton theon , with the article), and the Word was God ( theos , without the article)." Origen, the greatest Christian scholar of the 3rd century, explained the difference explicitly: John uses the article for the uncreated God, and leaves it off for the Word because the Word is "not God simply" but "god" in a derived sense, though more exalted than other "gods" ( Commentary on John 2.2).

 The Logos background. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish contemporary of Jesus, called the Logos "the second god", meaning a created intermediary, not YHWH. In the Hebrew Bible, God's "word" is His speech: "God said, let there be light" (Gen 1:3); "by the word of the LORD the heavens were made" (Ps 33:6). Proverbs 8 personifies Wisdom as a "she" who was with God and helped create, yet no one thinks Wisdom is a person of the godhead. John personifies God's creative word the same way, and that word became flesh in the sense that God's word was embodied in Jesus' life and message.

 Second-century readings. Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Hippolytus, Tertullian and Novatian held a "two-stage" Logos theology: the Word was internal to God, then at a point in time God "begot" or put forth the Word for creation. Theophilus says God "begot this Word… the first-born of all creation" ( To Autolycus 2.22). This makes the Son's existence as a distinct being begin , which Nicaea later condemned. So the earliest readers of John 1:1 did not read it as Nicene Christians do.

 "All things were made through him." This describes agency, not uncreated status. Eve is called "the mother of all living" (Gen 3:20) without being the source of life.

 Tap to enlarge Introduction to Justin Martyr: his Logos theology made the Word a subordinate "second God"
rows.obj:
"Colwell's rule: a definite predicate noun before the verb can drop the article and still be definite."
 Colwell's rule says definite predicates often lack the article, not that anarthrous predicates are definite. Most grammarians now read theos here as qualitative ("divine"), not "the God". Origen, a native Greek speaker, read it as lesser.


 "Jehovah's Witnesses say 'a god', and that's polytheism."
 We do not need "a god". The point is that the verse distinguishes the Word from "the God", and the Word is God's creative speech personified. Islam affirms that Jesus is "a word from Him" (3:45; 4:171) because he was created by God's command "Be".
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “John 1:14 says the Word "became flesh", so God became man.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer It says the Word became flesh, not "the God (ho theos)". The Quran says the same in its own way: Jesus is God's word, created by "Be" (3:59; 4:171). God's word taking effect in a human being is not God turning into a human.
rows.sum: John 1:1 distinguishes "the God" from the Word, who is "god" without the article. Origen read the Word as derived and lesser, Philo called the Logos a "second god", and the Hebrew background is God's spoken word personified, like Wisdom in Proverbs 8.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) is not a claim to be YHWH

rows.thesis: "I am" ( ego eimi ) is an ordinary Greek phrase used by other people in John; the divine name in the Greek Old Testament is a different phrase; and the context is about pre-existence or destiny, not deity.
rows.arg:
P1 For John 8:58 to identify Jesus with YHWH, "ego eimi" must be the divine name. 
 P2 In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), God's name in Exodus 3:14 is ho ōn ("the One who is"), not ego eimi . In John, a blind man says ego eimi of himself (9:9), and Jesus uses the phrase to mean "I am he" (the Messiah). 
 ∴ John 8:58 does not identify Jesus with YHWH.
rows.ev:
In the Septuagint, Exodus 3:14 reads " Ego eimi ho ōn ": "I am the One who is ". The name given to Moses is ho ōn , and the next clause is "tell them ho ōn has sent me". Ego eimi is just the Greek for "I am".

 The healed blind man says " ego eimi " ("I am the man") in John 9:9. Nobody thinks he claims to be God.

 In John, ego eimi is regularly messianic: to the Samaritan woman's "I know Messiah is coming", Jesus answers " Ego eimi , the one speaking to you" (4:26); "unless you believe that ego eimi , you will die in your sins" (8:24), explained by the purpose statement "these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ" (20:31). Mark 13:6 has "many will come in my name saying ego eimi ", and Matthew 24:5 interprets it: "saying, I am the Christ".

 The context is about Abraham seeing Jesus' day (8:56). At most it claims pre-existence or that he existed in God's plan, as in "the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world" (Rev 13:8) and Jeremiah, known before he was formed (Jer 1:5).

 Jesus bearing God's name is no proof either: in Exodus 23:21 God says of His angel, "My name is in him". Jesus says the name was given to him (John 17:11-12).
rows.obj:
"The Jews tried to stone him, so they knew he claimed to be God."
 The Jews in John also tried to stone him for other statements (10:31), and Jesus' own answer then was Psalm 82 and "Son of God", not "I am God". An angry crowd's reaction is not a definition of his words.


 "It's the present tense, 'I am' instead of 'I was', implying eternity."
 Greek uses the present for a state continuing from the past ("I have been"), as in John 14:9 ("so long a time I am with you"). Several translations render 8:58 "I have been" for this reason.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Isaiah uses "I am He" (ani hu, LXX ego eimi) as God's self-declaration, so John is echoing Isaiah.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer In Isaiah the declaration is "I am He, and there is no god besides Me" (Isa 43:10-11). If Jesus were echoing that, he would be denying any other god, including the Father he prays to. And the same phrase was used by the blind man. Echo needs more than two common words.
rows.sum: The divine name in the Greek Exodus 3:14 is ho ōn , not ego eimi . A blind man uses the same words in John 9:9, and elsewhere in John they mean "I am the Messiah". 8:58 is about Jesus' place in God's plan, not a claim to be God.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: Thomas' "My Lord and my God" and John 17:5

rows.thesis: Thomas' exclamation comes three verses after Jesus calls the Father "my God", and the "glory before the world" in John 17:5 is the standard Jewish idiom of predestination.
rows.arg:
P1 A verse must be read in its context and in its author's idiom. 
 P2 John 20:28 comes just after Jesus says "my God and your God" (20:17) and just before John states his purpose: that you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31). John 17:5 uses the same past-tense idiom the NT uses for things predestined. 
 ∴ Neither verse teaches that Jesus is God.
rows.ev:
John 20:28. Theodore of Mopsuestia, a major 4th-century bishop, read Thomas' words as an exclamation of praise to God at the sight of the miracle, like "My God!" today. (His reading was condemned only in 553, at the Second Council of Constantinople, which shows it had been a live Christian interpretation.) Within John, Jesus had already said that seeing him is seeing the Father because the Father does the works through him (14:9-10). And the author tells us why he included it: "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God" (20:31), not "that Jesus is God".

 John 17:5, "the glory I had with You before the world existed". The NT routinely describes God's plan in the past tense: grace "was given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Tim 1:9); the Lamb "slain from the foundation of the world" (Rev 13:8); believers "chosen before the foundation of the world" (Eph 1:4) and already "seated in the heavenly places" (Eph 2:6); Christ "foreknown before the foundation of the world" (1 Pet 1:20). Augustine ( Tractate 105) and others read 17:5 as the predestined glory of Jesus' human nature. In 17:22 Jesus says he has given the disciples the same glory. The Quran uses the same idiom: the infant Jesus says "He has given me the Book and made me a prophet" (19:30) of what lay in the future.
rows.ar:
قَالَ إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ وَجَعَلَنِي نَبِيًّا
 19:30
rows.obj:
"Jesus accepted Thomas' words without correcting him."
 He responds "Have you believed because you have seen me?" (20:29), praising faith, not endorsing a theology. If Thomas meant that Jesus was the God whom Jesus had just called "my God", the text would contradict itself three verses apart.


 "Pre-existence is different from predestination."
 Even if one insists on real pre-existence, that makes Jesus a created heavenly being before his birth, not the uncreated God. Arians believed in pre-existence too.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Thomas addressed Jesus directly ("he said to him"), so it can't be an exclamation to God.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Exclamations are often spoken to someone ("he said to him, 'Good heavens!'"). But grant that he addressed Jesus: John 10:34-35 shows that in John's own idiom human agents of God can be called "gods" (Psalm 82:6). John's stated purpose (20:31) defines the confession as Messiah and Son of God.
rows.sum: Thomas speaks three verses after Jesus says "my God and your God", and John says the point is to believe Jesus is the Messiah. The "glory before the world" uses the NT's ordinary language of predestination, the same idiom as Quran 19:30.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: Philippians 2:6-11: the second Adam, not God incarnate

rows.thesis: The hymn contrasts Jesus with Adam: Adam grasped at being like God; Jesus did not, humbled himself, and was rewarded by God with exaltation and a name. Someone who is God cannot be given exaltation.
rows.arg:
P1 God cannot be exalted or given a name by another, since He is already supreme. 
 P2 Philippians 2:9 says "God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name", "to the glory of God the Father" (2:11). 
 ∴ The hymn presents Jesus as a human being exalted by God for his obedience, not as God.
rows.ev:
Read the hymn against Genesis 3. Adam was made in God's image (Gen 1:27) and grasped at being "like God" (Gen 3:5). Jesus, "being in the form ( morphe ) of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped", but took the form of a servant and was obedient to death (Phil 2:6-8). Morphe is the outward appearance or status; Adam also bore God's image. The point is moral: the obedient second Adam versus the disobedient first.

 Then: " Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name" (2:9). The exaltation is a reward. Peter says the same: God "exalted him at His right hand" (Acts 2:33; 5:31). The whole act ends "to the glory of God the Father" (2:11), not to the glory of Jesus as God. The bowing of "every knee" echoes Isaiah 45:23, where it is directed to God; here it happens through the one God has exalted, to God's glory.
rows.obj:
"'Form of God' means he had the divine nature."
 If morphe means nature, then "form of a servant" (2:7) means he had a servant's nature, so his servanthood would be his essence. Most scholars read both as status or appearance.


 "'The name above every name' is YHWH, so Jesus is YHWH."
 The name is given to him, and the purpose clause is the glory of the Father. Angels in Scripture carry God's name ("My name is in him", Exod 23:21) without being God.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Paul says Jesus "emptied himself", so he had divinity to empty.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The same hymn says he took "the form of a servant", and in Paul's thought Jesus gave up status and privilege, as 2 Corinthians 8:9 says ("though he was rich, he became poor"). Nothing in the hymn says he emptied himself of being God, and the climax is that God exalted him, which makes no sense if he was God all along.
rows.sum: Philippians 2 contrasts Jesus' obedience with Adam's grasping, then says God exalted him and gave him a name, to the glory of the Father. Being exalted and given a name is what happens to a servant, not to God.

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: The "divine acts" of Jesus were done by prophets too

rows.thesis: Worship (proskuneo), forgiving sins, walking on water, knowing hearts, judging and receiving titles like "king of kings" are all given to human beings in the Bible, so none proves deity.
rows.arg:
P1 An act proves deity only if it is unique to God. 
 P2 Each of the acts cited for Jesus is performed or given to prophets, kings or angels elsewhere in the Bible, often explicitly "by God's authority". 
 ∴ These acts do not prove that Jesus is God.
rows.ev:
Homage. Proskuneo is given to King David (1 Chr 29:20, LXX) and to Joseph's brothers bowing to him (Gen 42:6).

 Walking on water. Peter walked on water too (Matt 14:29); Moses parted the sea and Elisha made iron float (2 Kgs 6:6).

 Raising the dead. Elijah (1 Kgs 17) and Elisha (2 Kgs 4) raised the dead; Elisha's bones raised a man (2 Kgs 13:21). The Quran says Jesus raised the dead "by Allah's permission" (5:110).

 Knowing hearts. Samuel knew Saul's thoughts (1 Sam 9:19-20), Ahijah knew the disguised queen (1 Kgs 14:6), Elisha knew what the king of Aram said in his bedroom (2 Kgs 6:12).

 Judging. "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son… because he is the son of man" (John 5:22, 27). The apostles will sit on twelve thrones judging Israel (Matt 19:28).

section_title: Jesus is not God in the New Testament
title: The Gospels' own prophecy citations create problems for a divine Jesus

rows.thesis: Several Old Testament passages the Gospels apply to Jesus, read in context, describe a sinner or a false prophet, which no Christian can accept of God.
rows.caution: This is a rhetorical, turn-the-tables argument. Use it to show the problems with Christian proof-texting from the OT, not as a claim about Jesus, whom Muslims honour as a sinless prophet.
rows.ev:
Matthew 26:31 applies Zechariah 13:7 ("strike the shepherd") to Jesus. The verses just before (13:3-6) are about false prophets wounded "in the house of my friends".

 John 13:18 applies Psalm 41:9 ("he who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me") to Judas and Jesus. The speaker of that psalm says, "heal me, for I have sinned against You" (41:4).

 Matthew 2:15 applies Hosea 11:1 ("out of Egypt I called my son") to Jesus. Hosea's "son" is Israel, which in the next verse "kept sacrificing to the Baals" (11:2).
rows.obj:
"Typology applies only part of a passage."
 Then the Gospel writers chose passages about sinful figures to prove their claims. Either context matters, in which case the passages do not fit, or it doesn't, in which case they prove nothing about Jesus.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “You are insulting Jesus.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer No, I am showing that the Gospel writers' method of citing the Old Testament does not work. Muslims believe Jesus was sinless. It is the Christian proof-texts, read in context, that would call him a sinner.
rows.sum: Zechariah 13:7, Psalm 41:9 and Hosea 11:1, read in context, describe a false prophet, a sinner and an idolatrous son. The Gospels' use of them shows their prophecy method ignores context.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: The Hebrew Bible teaches one God who is a single person

rows.thesis: The Old Testament speaks of God with singular pronouns and verbs thousands of times, says He created "alone, by Myself", and was never read as triune by the people it was given to.
rows.arg:
P1 If God were three persons, the revelation given to Israel would say so, or at least Israel would have understood it. 
 P2 The Old Testament insists God is one and alone, uses singular grammar for Him, and Jews have never read it as teaching three persons. Christian scholars admit the doctrine is not revealed there. 
 ∴ The Old Testament teaches unitarian monotheism, the same monotheism as the Quran.
rows.ev:
The Shema. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one ( echad )" (Deut 6:4). Echad is the ordinary Hebrew numeral "one": "God took one of his ribs" (Gen 2:21). The scholar S.R. Driver explains that the verse contrasts the one LORD with the many local Baals; it is about number, not a "compound unity".

 Alone. "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by Myself " (Isa 44:24). "I am the LORD and there is no other; besides Me there is no God" (Isa 45:5). "Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?" (Mal 2:10).

 Jesus' own Shema. When asked which commandment is first, Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 6:4 and the scribe replied, "You are right, Teacher, He is one and there is no other besides Him", and Jesus said he was "not far from the kingdom of God" (Mark 12:29-34).

 Christian concessions. The Catholic Encyclopedia states that the doctrine of the Trinity is not taught in the Old Testament, and Augustine saw it only as foreshadowed. Jews, the original readers, unanimously reject it.
rows.ar:
قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ۝ اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ ۝ لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ ۝ وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ
 112:1-4
rows.obj:
"Echad can mean a compound unity, like 'one flesh' (Gen 2:24) or 'one cluster'."
 The compound idea comes from the noun ("flesh", "cluster"), not from echad . "One flesh" is one flesh, not three persons. In the Shema, echad describes God Himself, and the rest of the Bible says He made things "alone".


 "Progressive revelation: God revealed the Trinity later."
 Revelation can add, but it cannot contradict. If God told Israel for 1,500 years that He is one and alone, and then revealed that He is three persons, the earlier revelation misled everyone who received it. That is not progress but reversal.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Jews didn't understand the Old Testament properly; that's why they rejected Jesus.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Then God spoke to Israel for centuries in a way that no one in Israel, prophet or scribe, understood. Even Jesus' own disciples in Acts call him "a man attested by God". It is more reasonable that the Jews understood their own scripture on its most basic point: who God is.
rows.sum: The Shema, "by Myself" (Isa 44:24) and "no other besides Me" (Isa 45:5) teach one God who is one person. Jesus affirmed the Shema, Jews never saw a Trinity, and Christian scholars admit the doctrine is not in the Old Testament.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: By Deuteronomy 13, a Trinitarian Jesus would be a false prophet

rows.thesis: The Torah tests every prophet: even if he works signs, if he calls Israel to a god they "have not known", he is false. A Jesus who demanded worship of himself as a divine Son would fail that test, so Christians must choose between the Trinity and the Torah.
rows.arg:
P1 Deuteronomy 13:1-5: a prophet who performs signs but says "let us follow other gods which you have not known" is false. 
 P2 Israel had never known a triune God or a divine Son to be worshipped; Jesus himself says the Jews worship "what we know" (John 4:22) and calls the Father "the one you say is your God" (John 8:54). 
 P3 The Trinitarian Jesus requires Israel to worship someone in addition to the God they knew. 
 ∴ If Jesus taught the Trinity, he fails Deuteronomy 13. Since Jesus was a true prophet, he did not teach it.
rows.ev:
The test in Deuteronomy 13 is decisive because it explicitly says signs are not enough: "If a prophet arises among you… and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign comes to pass, and he says, 'Let us go after other gods which you have not known'… you shall not listen to the words of that prophet" (13:1-3). The criterion is continuity with the God Israel already knew.

 Jesus himself defines that God: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews" (John 4:22, to the Samaritan). The God "we know" is the God of the Jews, who is one person. And he identifies the Father as the God the Jews claim: "It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God'" (John 8:54).

 This argument puts the Christian in a dilemma. Either the Trinity is a new revelation, in which case it introduces a God Israel did not know and fails Deuteronomy 13; or it is not new, in which case it should be visible in the Old Testament, and the rest of this section shows it is not.
rows.obj:
"It's not 'another god'; it's the same God more fully revealed."
 Israel knew God as one person, "He". A God who is three persons, one of whom is a man to be worshipped, is a different object of worship from the one Israel knew. Deuteronomy's phrase is "gods you have not known", and Israel had not known this one.


 "Jesus' miracles prove he was a true prophet."
 Deuteronomy 13 explicitly anticipates that a false prophet may perform signs. That is why the content of the message is the test.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Islam also brought something new: Muhammad. Doesn't he fail Deuteronomy 13?”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer No. He called to the God Israel knew: one, without partner, the God of Abraham and Moses. Deuteronomy 13 forbids new gods, not new prophets; Deuteronomy 18:18 promises a new prophet. Muhammad passes the test the Trinity fails.
rows.sum: Deuteronomy 13 says even a miracle-working prophet is false if he calls to a god Israel had not known. Israel never knew a triune God, so a Trinitarian Jesus would fail the Torah's own test. The Muslim Jesus, who called to the one God, passes it.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: The Angel of the LORD is God's messenger, not God

rows.thesis: When the Angel of the LORD speaks in the first person for God, he is doing what every messenger in the ancient world did: speaking in the voice of the one who sent him.
rows.arg:
P1 In the Bible and the ancient Near East, an agent speaks in the first person for his principal; prophets and royal messengers do it routinely. 
 P2 The Angel of the LORD is called a messenger ( mal'akh ), is sent, and speaks God's words. The Bible says God appeared face to face only to Moses, while the Angel appears visibly to many. 
 ∴ The Angel of the LORD is a messenger speaking for God, not God Himself.
rows.ev:
First-person agency is normal. A prophet in Judges 6:8-10 says "Thus says the LORD… I brought you up from Egypt". David's messengers speak to Abigail in David's name, and she bows to them and calls herself David's servant (1 Sam 25:40-41). Abner's messengers speak in the first person for Abner (2 Sam 3:12). In Genesis 22:15-16 the angel says "By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD ", which is quoting God, not being Him.

 God's appearance is limited. In Numbers 12:6-8 God says He reveals Himself to prophets only in visions and dreams, but to Moses "mouth to mouth". Yet the Angel of the LORD appears physically to Hagar, Gideon, Manoah and his wife, and others. If the Angel were God, God would be appearing face to face to many, contradicting Numbers 12.

 The NT reads it as an angel. Stephen says that at the burning bush "an angel appeared to him in the flame of fire", through whom God spoke (Acts 7:30-35). Agency also explains the switch between 2 Samuel 24:1 (the LORD incited David) and 1 Chronicles 21:1 (Satan incited David): the act of an agent can be ascribed to the one who allows or sends it.

 The usual "divine" features are shared. "Obey his voice… My name is in him" (Exod 23:21): God's name is placed in Jerusalem, the Temple and Israel (Jer 14:9) too. People bow to him: they also bow to David and Joseph, and Jacob tells Esau "seeing your face is like seeing the face of God" (Gen 33:10). Manoah fears death "because we have seen God", but Pharaoh also told Moses that whoever saw his face again would die (Exod 10:28). Holy ground: there are holy nations, holy angels and holy lands.

 Tap to enlarge Biblical scholarship: the Angel of YHWH is a messenger who speaks for God, not God himself
rows.obj:
"In Exodus 3 the angel says 'I am the God of Abraham'."
 That is first-person agency, exactly as the prophet in Judges 6 says "I brought you up from Egypt". Acts 7:30-35 says it was an angel through whom God spoke.


 "The angel accepts worship and sacrifice (Judges 13)."
 In Judges 13:16 the angel tells Manoah: "If you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD ". He refuses the offering for himself.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “The Angel of the LORD disappears after Jesus is born, which shows he was the pre-incarnate Christ.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer An "angel of the Lord" appears repeatedly in the NT after Jesus' birth: to Joseph (Matt 1:20, 2:13), the shepherds (Luke 2:9), Peter in prison (Acts 12:7). He did not disappear.
rows.sum: Messengers speak in their sender's voice; the Angel is sent, says "declares the LORD", and refuses offerings for himself; God appears face to face only to Moses (Num 12). Stephen calls the bush figure an angel.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: Plural words ("Elohim", "Let us") do not mean plural persons

rows.thesis: Hebrew uses plurals for majesty and excellence, and God addresses His heavenly court. If "Let us" proved three persons, the same reasoning would make many humans plural.
rows.arg:
P1 A plural form proves plural persons only if the language never uses plurals for a single person. 
 P2 Hebrew uses elohim for Moses and for a single pagan god, uses plural forms for one master, and the Bible shows God speaking to His council of angels. 
 ∴ The plurals do not imply a Trinity.
rows.ev:
"Elohim" with singular verbs. In Genesis 1:1, Elohim takes a singular verb ( bara , "He created"). The same word is used for Moses: "I have made you elohim to Pharaoh" (Exod 7:1), for a single pagan god (Chemosh, Judges 11:24), and for the ghost of Samuel, with a plural verb (1 Sam 28:13).

 Plurals of majesty and excellence. "Remember your Creators " (Eccl 12:1, a plural form in Hebrew); "your Makers is your Husbands " (Isa 54:5, plural forms for one God). Kings speak this way: King Artaxerxes writes "the letter you sent us " (Ezra 4:18), and Laban says " we will give you" (Gen 29:27).

 "Let us make man" (Gen 1:26). Many Jewish and some Christian commentators read this as God addressing the heavenly court, which the Bible describes elsewhere: "the sons of God shouted for joy" at creation (Job 38:7), "the host of heaven standing beside Him" (1 Kgs 22:19). Isaiah 6:8 has the same shift: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us ?" The very next verse (Gen 1:27) is singular: " God created man in His image". And Isaiah 44:24 says He made everything "alone".

 
 Tap to enlarge JPS Torah Commentary on Genesis 1:26: "Let us make" addresses the divine council, not a Trinity 
 
 The three men visit Abraham (Gen 18). Two of the three are explicitly called "the two angels" when they arrive in Sodom (Gen 19:1). Augustine ( City of God 16.29) read all three as angels, and Hebrews 13:2 alludes to it: "some have entertained angels unawares". Abraham bows to them as Jacob bowed to Esau.

 "The LORD rained… from the LORD" (Gen 19:24). Restating the name is Hebrew style: King Solomon says "to King Solomon" of himself (1 Kgs 8:1), and Jonathan says "the LORD God of Israel… when I have sounded my father" (1 Sam 20:12).
rows.obj:
"God can't be addressing angels, because man is made in God's image, not angels' image."
 Verse 27 says God created man "in His image", singular, showing the image is God's alone. Including the court in the announcement of a royal decree is natural.


 "Plural of majesty didn't exist in early Hebrew."
 It doesn't need to be a grammatical rule; the Bible shows plural words used for one person (Exod 7:1, 1 Sam 28:13, Isa 54:5) and kings using "we". And even if "us" were plural persons, it gives no number three.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “"Let us" shows more than one person in God, and nothing else in creation could be God's co-creator.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The next verse says "God created man in His image", singular, and Isaiah 44:24 says God made all things "alone, by Myself". If "us" meant co-creators, Isaiah would be false. A council being addressed is not a council creating.
rows.sum: Elohim is used for Moses and a pagan god and takes singular verbs for God; "Let us" is addressed to the heavenly court and followed by "His image"; the three visitors are angels (Gen 19:1). None of these teaches three persons.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: Psalms 45 and 110 are about Israel's king

rows.thesis: "Your throne, O God" (Ps 45:6) and "The LORD said to my lord" (Ps 110:1) are royal psalms about the human king, who has a God above him.
rows.arg:
P1 A psalm addressed to a human king, who is then told that God is his God, cannot be about God. 
 P2 Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song in which "God, your God, has anointed you" (45:7). Psalm 110 uses adoni ("my lord"), the form used for human masters and kings, not Adonai . 
 ∴ Neither psalm shows a second divine person.
rows.ev:
Psalm 45. Its own heading calls it a love song for the king's wedding. The king is praised for his beauty, his sword and his bride. Verse 6, "Your throne, O God, is forever", is followed by " God, your God , has anointed you above your companions" (v. 7). The king has a God over him. Elohim is used for human rulers (Exod 7:1; Ps 82:6), and Solomon sat on "the throne of the LORD" (1 Chr 29:23). Robert Alter translates it "your throne of God", and the NRSV Study Bible notes that the king is nowhere else called God.

 Psalm 110. "YHWH said to adoni : sit at my right hand till I make your enemies your footstool." In the Masoretic text, adoni is used throughout the Hebrew Bible for human lords (Sarah calls Abraham adoni ; subjects call the king adoni ), while God is Adonai . The details fit a Davidic king: enemies made a footstool (David in 2 Sam 22:39-41; "the LORD put them under the soles of his feet", 1 Kgs 5:3), the right hand as a place of honour (Bathsheba at Solomon's right hand, 1 Kgs 2:19), and priestly acts by David (he wore the ephod, offered sacrifices and blessed the people, 2 Sam 6:13-18). Herbert Bateman's study reads it as a royal psalm with the human king subordinate to God.

 Tap to enlarge Herbert Bateman, Psalm 110:1 and the New Testament: a royal psalm about the Davidic king, subordinate to God
rows.obj:
"Jesus used Psalm 110 to show the Messiah is more than David's son (Mark 12:35-37)."
 At most that shows the Messiah is greater than David, which Muslims accept of Jesus as a great prophet. It does not show he is YHWH; YHWH is the one speaking to him.


 "The vowel points that make it 'adoni' were added later by the Masoretes."
 True, but every ancient reading tradition, including the Septuagint's to kyrio mou ("to my lord"), distinguishes the speaker YHWH from the one addressed. Two parties are present whatever the vowels.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Hebrews 1:8 applies Psalm 45 to Jesus and calls him God.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Hebrews quotes the whole passage, including "God, your God, has anointed you" (Heb 1:9). Even in Hebrews, the one addressed has a God above him, so the application proves subordination, not deity.
rows.sum: Psalm 45 is a wedding song to the king, whose God anoints him; Psalm 110 has YHWH speaking to "my lord", a title for humans, with every detail fitting David's dynasty.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: Isaiah 9:6, 48:16 and 63:9

rows.thesis: The "Mighty God" child, the speaker "sent with His Spirit", and the "angel of His presence" are each explained by their context and by ancient readings without a Trinity.
rows.arg:
P1 A proof text for the Trinity must not have a natural reading in context without it. 
 P2 Isaiah 9:6 is a royal throne name (with Hebrew names routinely containing God's name); 48:16 has a speaker sent by God; and 63:9 in the Septuagint denies that an angel saved Israel. 
 ∴ None of these verses teaches the Trinity.
rows.ev:
Isaiah 9:6. "His name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God ( El Gibbor ), Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." Hebrew names often contain God's name or describe God: Elijah means "my God is YHWH", Jehu "YHWH is he". Jewish translations read the verse as "the Wonderful Counsellor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father has called his name Prince of Peace". The Septuagint renders it "his name is called Messenger of Great Counsel". The phrase el gibbor is used in the plural of human warriors ( elei gibborim , Ezek 32:21). Scholars such as John Hayes read the names as royal coronation titles of the kind given to Egyptian kings, applied to a Judean king (Hezekiah fits the context, 2 Kgs 18-20). And note: if the child is "Everlasting Father ", the verse would make the Son the Father, which Trinitarians deny.

 Isaiah 48:16. "The Lord GOD has sent me, and His Spirit." The speaker in context is the prophet, or the one God called (Cyrus, 44:28-45:1). The verb "sent me" is singular, so "His Spirit" is what the speaker is sent with , as scholars like Childs, Blenkinsopp and Goldingay translate: "has sent me with His Spirit". Sudden changes of speaker are common in the prophets.

 Isaiah 63:9-10. The Hebrew says "the angel of His presence saved them… but they rebelled and grieved His holy spirit". The parallel suggests the angel and the holy spirit are the same messenger (compare Exod 23:21, "do not rebel against him", said of the angel; Gabriel "stands in the presence of God", Luke 1:19). The Septuagint reads: "not an ambassador, nor a messenger, but he himself saved them", which distinguishes God from any angel. Either way, the passage is about God and His messenger, not three persons.

 Tap to enlarge Isaiah 63:9 in the Septuagint: "not an ambassador, nor a messenger, but he himself saved them"
rows.obj:
"Only God is called 'El Gibbor' in Isaiah 10:21."
 In 10:21 it describes God, but names that describe God are given to humans throughout the Bible. The question is whether the verse says the child is El Gibbor or is named with it, and Hebrew naming practice favours the second.


 "Isaiah 9:7 says his kingdom will have no end."
 God promises the same to David's line: "your throne shall be established forever" (2 Sam 7:16), which no one takes to mean David's sons are God.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Muslims can't explain why a mere child would be called "Mighty God".”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Hebrew names routinely carry God's name and describe God: Elijah, "my God is YHWH". By the same logic Elijah would be God. The Septuagint, the oldest translation, didn't even render it as "Mighty God".
rows.sum: Isaiah 9:6 is a royal name and, read literally, would make the Son the Father; 48:16 has a speaker "sent with His Spirit"; 63:9 in the Septuagint says no messenger but God saved them.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: Daniel, Micah, Zechariah and Malachi

rows.thesis: The "son of the gods" in Daniel 3, the "son of man" in Daniel 7, the ruler from Bethlehem in Micah 5:2 and the speakers in Zechariah are angels or human figures, not God.
rows.arg:
P1 A figure who is sent, given dominion, or has an origin cannot be the eternal, self-sufficient God. 
 P2 Daniel 3:25's figure is called an angel in 3:28; the son of man in Daniel 7 is given dominion and the kingdom then goes to "the saints"; Micah 5:2's ruler has "origins"; Zechariah's speaker says "the LORD has sent me". 
 ∴ These passages describe created agents.
rows.ev:
Daniel 3:25. Nebuchadnezzar sees a fourth figure "like a son of the gods" (Aramaic bar elahin ), then explains in verse 28: God "sent His angel and delivered His servants".

 Daniel 7:13-14. One "like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion, glory and a kingdom that all peoples "serve". God gave the same to Nebuchadnezzar: "the God of heaven has given you the kingdom… all peoples… shall serve him" (Dan 2:37-38; Jer 27:6-7). And Daniel's own interpretation says the kingdom is given "to the people of the saints of the Most High" (7:27). The Aramaic verb for "serve" ( pelach ) is used of serving in the Temple (Ezra 7:24) and of serving humans (Targum of Gen 27:29).

 Micah 5:2. "From you, Bethlehem, shall come forth for Me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose origins ( motsa'otav ) are from of old, from ancient days." An eternal God does not have "origins". "Days of old" describes David's era elsewhere ("I will raise up the booth of David… as in the days of old", Amos 9:11): the ruler comes from David's ancient line.

 Zechariah 2:8-11. The speaker says "you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me", the same formula that validates the prophet in Zechariah 4:9. A sent one is not the sender.

 Malachi 3:1. "I send My messenger to prepare the way before Me." Malachi 4:5 names him: Elijah, whom Jesus identifies with John the Baptist (Matt 11:14). Mark 1:2-3 merges this with Isaiah 40:3 and Exodus 23:20.

 
 Tap to enlarge Joel Marcus (Anchor Bible): Mark 1:2-3 merges Exodus 23:20, Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 
 
 Solomon's prayer. "Will God indeed dwell on the earth? Heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain You" (1 Kgs 8:27). God sends His Spirit through the prophets (Neh 9:30), not as a co-equal person.
rows.obj:
"Only God rides the clouds, so the son of man is divine."
 The figure comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days; he is brought, not enthroned by right. Clouds also accompany angels (Rev 10:1).


 "Jesus identified himself with the son of man."
 Muslims accept Jesus as a figure of honour exalted by God. Daniel 7 has him receive dominion from God, which supports the Muslim view.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Micah 5:2 says the ruler is "from everlasting", so he is eternal.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Hebrew mi-yemei 'olam means "from ancient days", the same phrase used for David's time (Amos 9:11). And the word before it is "origins", which no eternal being has.
rows.sum: Daniel 3:25's figure is an angel (3:28); Daniel 7's son of man receives dominion that also goes to the saints; Micah 5:2's ruler has "origins"; Zechariah's speaker is "sent"; Malachi's messenger is Elijah. None is God.

section_title: The "Trinity in the Old Testament" refuted
title: The Quran's method with earlier scripture is the Church's own

rows.thesis: Christians accuse the Quran of picking and choosing from earlier scripture, but the early church judged non-canonical books the same way: true in parts, false in others, tested against a standard.
rows.arg:
P1 If it is legitimate for Christians to judge a text "partly true, partly corrupted" by a standard, it is legitimate for the Quran. 
 P2 The early church did exactly that with the Gospel of Peter, Enoch, the apocrypha and other writings. 
 ∴ The Quran's role as muhaymin (5:48), confirming what is true and correcting what is false, is a recognised method, not an inconsistency.
rows.ev:
Bishop Serapion of Antioch (c. 200) said of the Gospel of Peter that "most of it belongs to the true teaching of the Saviour, but some things are additions" (Eusebius, Church History 6.12).

 Augustine ( City of God 15.23) said the apocrypha contain "some truth" but much falsehood.

 The NT itself quotes non-canonical sources: Jude 14 quotes the Book of Enoch as genuine prophecy; Acts 20:35 quotes a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels. John says much of what Jesus did is not written (John 21:25).

 Athanasius' Festal Letter 39 (367) classed books into canon, books to read for instruction, and apocrypha.

section_title: How the Trinity developed
title: Mainstream scholars agree the New Testament does not teach the Trinity

rows.thesis: Christian and secular scholars broadly agree that Jesus did not teach the Trinity, that no NT writer held it consciously, and that it was formulated in the 4th century.

 Tap to enlarge "No responsible New Testament scholar would claim that the doctrine of the Trinity was taught by Jesus"

section_title: How the Trinity developed
title: The early church fathers were not Trinitarians

rows.thesis: Nearly every major Christian writer before Nicaea taught that the Son was subordinate to the Father, came into existence by the Father's will, or was in some sense created. By the standard of 381 they were heretics.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Trinity were the original apostolic faith, the fathers closest to the apostles would teach it. 
 P2 The 2nd- and 3rd-century fathers taught that the Father alone is uncreated, that the Son was begotten by an act of the Father's will at a point in time, and that the Son is lower than the Father. 
 ∴ The Trinity was not the faith of the early church; it developed later.
rows.ev:
1 Clement 59:4 (c. 96), the earliest Christian writing outside the NT: "that all nations may know that You are God alone , and Jesus Christ is Your Son".

 Ignatius (c. 110): Jesus is "Son of God according to the will and power of God" ( Smyrnaeans 1). The later "long recension" of his letters inflates his Christology. Cardinal Newman admitted: "Ignatius may be considered a Patripassian, Justin arianizes, and Hippolytus is a Photinian."

 The Shepherd of Hermas (2nd century): the Son is exalted for his obedience, and the Holy Spirit is identified with the Son.

 Justin Martyr (c. 150): the Logos is "another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things" ( Dialogue 56), begotten "by an act of the Father's will" ( Dialogue 61, 128), and the Father cannot appear on earth while the Son can ( Dialogue 127). He lists the angels among those Christians "worship and adore" ( 1 Apology 6). The Catholic Encyclopedia speaks of his "unfortunate concepts of the temporal and voluntary generation of the Word, and subordinationism".

 
 Tap to enlarge Introduction to Justin Martyr's Logos theology: a subordinate "second God" begotten by the Father's will 
 
 Irenaeus (c. 180): the Son "received dominion from His Father" ( Against Heresies 3.6.1), and the Father excels the Son in knowledge (2.28).

 Theophilus of Antioch , the first to use the word trias ("triad": God, His Word, His Wisdom), says God "begot" the Word before creation ( To Autolycus 2.10, 2.22).

 Tertullian (c. 200), the first to use trinitas and persona : "there was a time when the Son was not" ( Against Hermogenes 3); "the Father is the entire substance, but the Son is a derivation and portion of the whole" ( Against Praxeas 9). He also admits that "the simple, who are always the majority of believers" accused him of preaching two or three gods ( Against Praxeas 3), which shows the ordinary Christian was unitarian.

 Origen (c. 230): "nothing is uncreated but the Father" ( Commentary on John 2.6); the Father's power is greater than the Son's, and the Son's than the Spirit's; and "we should not pray to any begotten being, not even to Christ himself, but only to the Father" ( On Prayer 15). He was anathematised in 553.

 Novatian : "the Father alone has no beginning" ( On the Trinity 31).

 Dionysius of Alexandria (c. 260): the Son is "a creature and made… alien in essence from the Father, as the vinedresser is from the vine". Even Athanasius admits he wrote this ( On the Opinion of Dionysius 4).

 Eusebius of Caesarea , the church historian who attended Nicaea: the Son is "not eternally coexistent with the Father" and is "Lord in the second degree" ( Demonstration of the Gospel 5.1; 4.15). Jerome called him the "most open defender of the heresy of Arius".

 Proverbs 8:22 , "The LORD created me at the beginning of His way", was applied to the Son by nearly all early fathers. Athanasius had to reinterpret it as referring to the incarnation once it became an Arian proof text.
rows.obj:
"They were working out the language; their faith was Trinitarian."
 Justin, Tertullian and Origen did not merely lack the words; they explicitly affirmed what Nicaea condemned: the Son begotten by will, a time when the Son was not, the Father alone uncreated. That is a different belief, not imprecise wording for the same one.


 "Gregory Thaumaturgus wrote a fully Trinitarian creed in the 3rd century."
 Scholars regard its Trinitarian articles as later: Moreschini and Norelli date the last two articles to the 4th century, Basil never cites them, and the Arabic text of the related treatise On the Trinity is classed as spurious (CPG 1787). Gregory's own teacher, Origen, contradicts it.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “The heretics were Arius and his followers. The fathers before them were orthodox.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Measured by Nicene orthodoxy, Justin's "another God subject to the Maker", Tertullian's "a time when the Son was not" and Origen's "do not pray to Christ" are exactly Arian positions. Arius did not invent subordinationism; he defended the older view.
rows.sum: From 1 Clement to Eusebius, the early fathers called the Father "God alone", said the Son was begotten by will, that there was a time when he was not, and that only the Father is uncreated. Tertullian even admits most believers thought his Trinity meant two or three gods.

section_title: How the Trinity developed
title: The Holy Spirit's divinity was undecided until 381

rows.thesis: As late as 380, Christian thinkers disagreed on whether the Holy Spirit was God, a creature or a divine power. Its co-equal status was decided by a council and enforced by imperial law.
rows.arg:
P1 A doctrine revealed by Jesus would not still be unsettled among leading Christians 350 years later. 
 P2 Gregory of Nazianzus, writing around 380, reports that Christian scholars variously held the Spirit to be an energy, a creature, God, or were unsure. Lactantius denied the Spirit was a distinct person. 
 ∴ The co-equal divinity of the Holy Spirit is a 4th-century development.
rows.ev:
Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the architects of the doctrine, says plainly: "Of the wise men among ourselves, some have conceived of Him as an Activity, some as a Creature, some as God, and some have been uncertain which to call Him" ( Oration 31.5, c. 380). The Council of Constantinople (381) settled the question, and Emperor Theodosius' edicts made it law, with penalties for dissenters.

 Earlier, Lactantius denied that the Spirit was a distinct person (Jerome, Letter 84), and the Shepherd of Hermas identified the Spirit with the Son. Biblically, Paul compares the Spirit of God to a man's own spirit inside him: "who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God" (1 Cor 2:11). A man's spirit is not a second person alongside him. In Hebrew parallelism the Spirit is God's breath and power (Ps 33:6; Job 33:4), and in the Quran al-Ruh al-Qudus is the angel Gabriel (16:102).
rows.ar:
قُلْ نَزَّلَهُ رُوحُ الْقُدُسِ مِن رَّبِّكَ بِالْحَقِّ
 16:102
rows.obj:
"The Spirit speaks and can be grieved (Eph 4:30), so it's a person."
 Wisdom also speaks and calls out in Proverbs 8, and blood "cries out" in Genesis 4:10. Personification is common. Besides, if personal language proves a person, Gabriel fits the description perfectly, as the Quran says.


 "Matthew 28:19 names the Spirit with Father and Son."
 Listing is not equality (1 Tim 5:21 lists God, Christ and the angels), and the triadic baptismal formula itself is textually doubtful (see Corruption of the Bible ).
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “If the Spirit's deity wasn't clear until 381, why do Christians say it's in the Bible?”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Exactly the right question. Gregory's own testimony shows that the Bible did not settle it for the best-read Christians of his day; a council did.

section_title: How the Trinity developed
title: The doctrine is logically incoherent

rows.thesis: The Trinity claims that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, the three are distinct, and there is only one God. These claims cannot all be true together under the ordinary meaning of "is".
rows.arg:
P1 If "the Father is God" and "the Son is God" express identity, and there is exactly one God, then the Father is the Son, by the logic of identity. 
 P2 The Trinity denies that the Father is the Son. 
 P3 If "is God" means only "is divine", then there are three divine individuals, which is three gods unless "God" names a shared nature rather than a person. 
 P4 But the God of the Bible is a person ("I", "He") who speaks, acts and loves, not an abstract nature. 
 ∴ Every way of reading the Trinity either collapses into one person (modalism), three gods (tritheism), or an impersonal "God", so the doctrine is incoherent.
rows.ev:
The classical statement of the problem is the "logical problem of the Trinity". Christian philosophers have proposed solutions, such as "relative identity" (the Father is the same God as the Son but not the same person ). Critics point out that relative identity abandons the normal logic of identity, and that God has properties that should transfer under identity: if the Father begot and the Son did not, they differ in a property, so they cannot be identical to the same thing.

 The incarnation adds a second problem. God is immutable: "I the LORD do not change" (Mal 3:6). If the Logos took on a human nature at a point in time, something about the Logos changed. If nothing changed, it is unclear what "became flesh" means.

 Christian thinkers have often conceded the point. Luther admitted that the Trinity and two natures are beyond and contrary to reason, to be accepted on faith. The church calls the doctrine a "mystery". But a mystery is something we cannot fully understand; a contradiction is something that cannot be true. The Quran's challenge is simple: "Say, He is Allah, One" (112:1), and "had there been gods besides Allah in the heavens and earth, they would have been ruined" (21:22).
rows.ar:
لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا
 21:22 
 لَّقَدْ كَفَرَ الَّذِينَ قَالُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ ثَالِثُ ثَلَاثَةٍ ۘ وَمَا مِنْ إِلَٰهٍ إِلَّا إِلَٰهٌ وَاحِدٌ
 5:73
rows.obj:
"Finite minds can't understand an infinite God."
 Agreed that we can't understand God fully, but we can know that contradictions are false. If finite minds cannot judge the Trinity, they also cannot judge it to be true. The Quran does not ask us to believe contradictions.


 "Three persons share one essence, like three humans share humanity."
 Three humans who share humanity are three humans. That analogy produces three gods.


 "The Trinity is like water: ice, liquid, steam."
 That is modalism (one thing in three states), which the church condemned. Most analogies end up as either modalism or tritheism.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “God is love, and love needs another person, so God must be more than one person.”

full_text:
Thesis
 The Trinity claims that the Father is God, the Son is God, the Spirit is God, the three are distinct, and there is only one God. These claims cannot all be true together under the ordinary meaning of "is".



 Argument
 P1 If "the Father is God" and "the Son is God" express identity, and there is exactly one God, then the Father is the Son, by the logic of identity. 
 P2 The Trinity denies that the Father is the Son. 
 P3 If "is God" means only "is divine", then there are three divine individuals, which is three gods unless "God" names a shared nature rather than a person. 
 P4 But the God of the Bible is a person ("I", "He") who speaks, acts and loves, not an abstract nature. 
 ∴ Every way of reading the Trinity either collapses into one person (modalism), three gods (tritheism), or an impersonal "God", so the doctrine is incoherent. 
 


 Evidence
 The classical statement of the problem is the "logical problem of the Trinity". Christian philosophers have proposed solutions, such as "relative identity" (the Father is the same God as the Son but not the same person ). Critics point out that relative identity abandons the normal logic of identity, and that God has properties that should transfer under identity: if the Father begot and the Son did not, they differ in a property, so they cannot be identical to the same thing.

 The incarnation adds a second problem. God is immutable: "I the LORD do not change" (Mal 3:6). If the Logos took on a human nature at a point in time, something about the Logos changed. If nothing changed, it is unclear what "became flesh" means.

 Christian thinkers have often conceded the point. Luther admitted that the Trinity and two natures are beyond and contrary to reason, to be accepted on faith. The church calls the doctrine a "mystery". But a mystery is something we cannot fully understand; a contradiction is something that cannot be true. The Quran's challenge is simple: "Say, He is Allah, One" (112:1), and "had there been gods besides Allah in the heavens and earth, they would have been ruined" (21:22).

 5:73 



 Objections
 "Finite minds can't understand an infinite God."
 Agreed that we can't understand God fully, but we can know that contradictions are false. If finite minds cannot judge the Trinity, they also cannot judge it to be true. The Quran does not ask us to believe contradictions.


 "Three persons share one essence, like three humans share humanity."
 Three humans who share humanity are three humans. That analogy produces three gods.


 "The Trinity is like water: ice, liquid, steam."
 That is modalism (one thing in three states), which the church condemned. Most analogies end up as either modalism or tritheism.

section_title: The crucifixion & resurrection
title: What the Quran actually claims

rows.thesis: The Quran denies that Jesus was killed or crucified, says the event was made to appear so, and says Allah raised him. This answers the Jewish boast and notes that the Christians themselves were "in doubt".
rows.arg:
P1 To refute a claim, you must first state it accurately. 
 P2 Quran 4:157 is a reply to a specific boast, "we killed the Messiah", and adds that "those who differ over it are in doubt about it, with no knowledge except following assumption". 
 ∴ The Quran's claim is precise: Jesus was not killed or crucified; it appeared so to observers; disputes about it rest on conjecture.
rows.ev:
The passage (4:153-158) is a list of the crimes of a group of the Children of Israel: breaking the covenant, killing prophets, slandering Mary with "a great calumny" (4:156), and saying "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah". The boast is real: the Babylonian Talmud has a tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu" (Sanhedrin 43a), and slanders about Mary appear in the same literature (Sanhedrin 106a).

 Shubbiha lahum means "it was made to look like that to them". Commentators differ on how: one view is that another man was given his likeness (the substitution view), another that the scene was confused and people thought he had died. Both fit the text. The phrase "those who differ over it are in doubt" fits the Christians, who in the first centuries disagreed sharply about what happened at the cross (see below).
rows.ar:
وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا الْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ابْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ اخْتَلَفُوا فِيهِ لَفِي شَكٍّ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا اتِّبَاعَ الظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًا
 4:157 
 بَلْ رَّفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ ۚ وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَزِيزًا حَكِيمًا
 4:158
rows.obj:
"God deceived everyone, which is immoral."
 God protected His messenger from his enemies, as He did Lot and Abraham. Those who plotted to kill him were the ones deceived about their success; the Quran calls it Allah's plan against their plan (3:54). Jesus' followers were not commanded to believe anything false; the later doctrine of the cross was built on assumption, as the verse says.


 "Why would God let Christianity be built on a mistake for 600 years?"
 The early Jesus movement was not uniformly built on the cross (see the next arguments), and the Quran came to settle the disagreement. Every prophet came to correct errors that had grown up after the previous one.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “If 4:157 is true, God founded Christianity on a deception.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The deception was of the plotters, who thought they had won. Christianity's doctrine of atonement was built by later teachers, mainly Paul, on top of what was "made to appear". The Quran says the people who disputed it were following conjecture, and the earliest records show exactly that dispute.
rows.sum: The Quran answers a boast that "we killed the Messiah": he was not killed or crucified, it was made to appear so, and Allah raised him. It says those who differ over the event follow conjecture.

section_title: The crucifixion & resurrection
title: The earliest Jesus sources say nothing of the crucifixion or resurrection

rows.thesis: The oldest reconstructable layers of the Jesus tradition (the Q sayings source, the Gospel of Thomas, the Epistle of James) have no passion narrative and no resurrection, and the passion predictions in the Gospels look like later additions.
rows.arg:
P1 If the crucifixion and resurrection were the centre of Jesus' own message, the earliest collections of his teaching would contain them. 
 P2 Q, Thomas and James contain no account of his death or resurrection; the disciples in the Gospels behave as if Jesus never predicted them; and Mark, the earliest Gospel, originally ended with no resurrection appearance. 
 ∴ The crucifixion-resurrection message was not part of the earliest teaching tradition; it was built up later.
rows.ev:
Q. The sayings source shared by Matthew and Luke (about 4,500 words) has no passion narrative and no resurrection. John Kloppenborg calls this "the most striking difference" between Q and the Gospels.

 The Gospel of Thomas , 114 sayings of Jesus, has no account of the crucifixion and no resurrection appearances.

 The Epistle of James , from Jesus' own brother and the leader of the Jerusalem church, never mentions the cross, the resurrection or atonement.

 Mark's ending. The earliest manuscripts of Mark (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) end at 16:8: the women flee from the empty tomb "and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid". There is no appearance of the risen Jesus. Verses 9-20 were added later.

 Passion predictions. Jesus predicts his death and rising on the third day again and again (Mark 8:31, 9:31, 10:33-34). Yet at his arrest the disciples flee, no one goes to the tomb expecting a resurrection, the women bring spices to anoint a corpse, and the disciples dismiss the women's report as "nonsense" (Luke 24:11). That behaviour makes sense only if the predictions were not made. Scholars from Bultmann to Vermes regard them as written after the fact. The Oxford Bible Commentary on Mark says they "owe a lot to later Christian creativity".

 
 Tap to enlarge Commentary on Mark: the passion predictions "owe a lot to later Christian creativity" 
 Tap to enlarge Geza Vermes: the resurrection was not among the central tenets of Jesus' teaching 
 
 No atonement in Luke-Acts. Bart Ehrman notes that Luke removes Mark's "ransom for many" (Mark 10:45) and that the sermons in Acts present Jesus' death as a miscarriage of justice reversed by God, not as an atoning sacrifice.
rows.obj:
"Q is a sayings collection; you wouldn't expect a narrative."
 That is the point: the earliest followers preserved Jesus' teaching , and his teaching did not centre on a coming atoning death. If the cross were the core of the message, it would appear among the sayings.


 "Mark 16:8 implies the resurrection through the empty tomb."
 An empty tomb is exactly what the Quran's account produces: Jesus was raised. It is not evidence of a death followed by resurrection.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Paul's creed in 1 Corinthians 15 dates to within a few years of the crucifixion, so the belief is early.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Early belief is consistent with the Quran: it appeared so to them. But the creed has its own problems: it names "the Twelve" when Judas was dead, omits the women and the empty tomb, and its witnesses (like the 500) are unnamed. Paul's own "appearance" was a light and a voice (Acts 26:13-19).
rows.sum: Q, Thomas and James have no passion or resurrection; Mark originally ended without any appearance; and the disciples act as if Jesus never predicted his death. The cross-centred message developed later.
